text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London ended lower after speculative liquidation in New York extended to the European market. May ended $1.90 lower at $307.10 per tonne, while August gave up $2.10 to close at $306.00 per tonne. In New York raw sugar futures closed lower across the board in a technically motivated session. May lost 13 points to close at 10.84 cents/lb, while July shed 8 points to close at 10.64 cents/lb. The outer months lost 10 to 12 points.

However, prices are still noticeably above the 10 cents/lb predicted by the ISO. Recent strength has been driven by a friendlier physical market with purchases by Iran (possible as much as 300,000 tonnes in the last three months) and Iraq, which is expected to be a buyer under the UN oil-for-food deal and has set a tender for 120,000 tonnes of white sugar. China is also being reported buying sugar for re-export. Adding to the strength was a report that Brazil has removed the tax- exemption for the extra 500,000 tonnes of sugar exports expected for 1996/97 and put it back into the domestic market. However, the overall picture is still for a significant surplus, most of which, however, is locked up in India.

CHINA - According to industry sources sugar production in 1996/97 (September/August) may be somewhat lower than had been expected. The total is now put at 7.1 million tonnes, still up from last year's figure of 6.8 million tonnes and the 1994/95 total of 5.9 million tonnes. Of the total expected to be produced in 1996/97 beet sugar may account for 1.463 million tonnes and cane sugar for 5.624 million tonnes.

GERMANY - Sugar consumption in January 1997 reached a healthy 250,537 tonnes, raw value, up from last year's 238,312 tonnes. This brought cumulative consumption in the first four months of 1996/97 (October/January) up to 991,076 tonnes, hardly changed from last year's 991,323 tonnes. Total consumption in 1995/96 amounted to 3.076 million tonnes compared to 2.995 million tonnes in 1994/95 and 2.940 million tonnes in 1993/94. Sugar output in January 1997 reached 10,503 tonnes, up from last year's 5,196 tonnes. This brought cumulative production in October/January 1996/97 up to 4.543 million tonnes compared to 4.136 million tonnes in the corresponding period the previous year. Total production in 1995/96 amounted to 4.158 million tonnes compared to 3.991 million tonnes in 1994/95.

FRANCE - Sugar consumption in October 1996 reached 215,692 tonnes, raw value, sharply up from last year's 179,843 tonnes. Total consumption in 1995/96 (October/September) reached 2.214 million tonnes compared to 2.184 million tonnes in 1994/95 and 2.208 million tonnes in 1993/94.

JAPAN - Sugar imports in December 1996 amounted to 134,687 tonnes, raw value, up from last year's 120,609 tonnes. This brought cumulative imports in the first quarter of 1996/97 (October/December) up to 504,851 tonnes, down from 521,147 tonnes imported in the like period the previous year. Total imports in 1995/96 (October/September) reached 1.681 million tonnes, down from 1.716 million tonnes in 1994/96 and 1.704 million tonnes in 1993/94. Major countries of origin in October/December 1996 were Australia with 301,049 tonnes raws against 295,900 tonnes, South Africa with 91,095 tonnes, down from 129,768 tonnes, Thailand with 56,500 tonnes compared to 94,296 tonnes and Fiji with 54,765 tonnes compared to nil.

NORWAY - Sugar imports in January 1997 amounted to 11,632 tonnes, raw value, compared to 12,342 tonnes in January 1996. Total imports in 1996 reached 188,832 tonnes compared to 173,712 tonnes in 1995 and 192,368 tonnes in 1994. Major countries of origin in January 1997 were Denmark with 5,578 tonnes whites against 8,354 tonnes and the UK with 2,241 tonnes compared to 2,427 tonnes. TENDERS
Bangladesh bought one cargo of 150 ICUMSA low quality white sugar at around $346 per tonne c&f for shipment March 11/April 11.
